title: The Terminal of Station Meridian
premise: Gideon Zhou is the last active terraformer aboard Station Meridian, tending a greenhouse garden commissioned for colonists who will never arrive, recording daily logs of a station everyone else has written off. When he finds an impossible name—his own dead sister's—on the manifest of a ship that never flew, he uncovers a decades-old deception: the truce between two rival fleets orbiting Meridian rests on forged records he unknowingly inherited. As the truce's expiration nears and both fleets converge to claim the station, Gideon must decide whether to expose the lie and shatter the peace or become its living author. In the end, he chooses neither truth nor lie but testimony: he broadcasts the full archive—the garden, the logs, the forgery—and the fleets, confronted with the people they abandoned, sign a new charter naming Meridian a shared sanctuary, with Gideon as its first keeper.
about_author: Yara Marchetti is a former hydroponics technician who spent six years on orbital agricultural projects before turning to fiction. She writes quiet, character-driven science fiction about the people maintenance leaves behind.

chapters.title: The Garden for No One
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. He tends the terraforming greenhouse alone, recording log entry 4,000 for colonists who never came, establishing his routines, his loneliness, and his stubborn devotion. Emotional beat: tender melancholy—the comfort of purpose without an audience.

chapters.title: Manifest Anomalies
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. While archiving old shipping records, he finds the Meridian Star listed as never flown—yet bearing a passenger manifest, including the name Lin Zhou, his sister, dead twenty years. Emotional beat: cold shock cracking open old grief.

chapters.title: What the Station Remembers
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. He searches sealed archives and finds the manifest repeated across official fleet documents, too consistent to be error. Someone built the lie deliberately. Emotional beat: dawning unease; the station feels suddenly watchful.

chapters.title: The Truce Clock
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. A routine broadcast reveals the fleet truce expires in ninety days, and both rival fleets have scheduled 'administrative visits' to Meridian. Emotional beat: dread; his invisible life now sits on a countdown.

chapters.title: Visitor from the Verge
chapters.summary: Introduces Captain Oyelaran of the Verge Fleet, arriving early under inspection pretense, probing Gideon about station records. First meeting: wary politeness masking interrogation. Emotional beat: Gideon realizes he is being measured, not seen.

chapters.title: Lin Zhou, Passenger
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Digging into the forged manifest, he discovers entries in his mother's handwriting style—she helped forge passenger lists to smuggle refugees off a dying world, and Lin's name was added posthumously as cover. Emotional beat: grief transmuted into furious questions.

chapters.title: The Second Fleet Knocks
chapters.summary: Commander Ashke of the Halcyon Fleet arrives unannounced, equally interested in the archives, and far less polite. The two visitors nearly clash in the docking bay while Gideon stands between them. Emotional beat: terror and a strange thrill—he matters to someone at last.

chapters.title: Tea with a Spy
chapters.summary: Oyelaran's POV. She admits, obliquely, that her fleet knows the truce rests on fabricated refugee manifests and needs the originals intact before expiry. She offers Gideon protection. Emotional beat: seduction of alliance; trust offered like a trap.

chapters.title: Rootstock
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. He grafts new cuttings in the garden and works through what his mother did: she saved forty families by inventing passengers, making Meridian legally obligated to both fleets. Emotional beat: reluctant pride braided with resentment at inheriting her burden.

chapters.title: Ashke's Ultimatum
chapters.summary: Ashke's POV. He demands Gideon hand over the archive, revealing Halcyon plans to void the truce and claim Meridian outright if the forgery surfaces first. Emotional beat: menace; Gideon understands both fleets see him as a key, not a person.

chapters.title: The Log Nobody Read
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Reviewing his own 4,000 entries, he realizes his daily recordings are themselves an archive of abandonment—evidence no one asked for. He decides to finish reading his mother's letters before choosing sides. Emotional beat: resolve kindling from self-recognition.

chapters.title: Letters from the Dying World
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. His mother's letters reveal she stayed behind so others could flee, asking Gideon—then a child—to keep the garden alive 'for whoever finally comes.' Emotional beat: devastating tenderness; the garden was always a promise, not a memorial.

chapters.title: Sabotage in Sector Nine
chapters.summary: Oyelaran's POV. Someone destroys part of the archive vault; suspicion falls on Gideon, then on a third party—a faction inside Oyelaran's own fleet wanting the truce broken. Emotional beat: paranoia; allies fracture.

chapters.title: The Name on the Door
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. He finds evidence the saboteur used credentials belonging to Lin Zhou—someone has been living inside his sister's identity aboard Meridian for years. Emotional beat: vertigo; the dead may be walking his corridors.

chapters.title: Mira
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Gideon corners the intruder: Mira, a stowaway's daughter raised on forged identities, who kept Lin's name alive because it opened doors no orphan could otherwise knock on. Emotional beat: recognition—two children of the same lie finding each other.

chapters.title: Ninety Days, Spent
chapters.summary: Ensemble. With days left, Gideon convenes Oyelaran, Ashke, and Mira in the greenhouse, laying out the whole forgery. Accusations fly; the truce's true origin—mutual shame, not mutual threat—surfaces. Emotional beat: raw confrontation becoming reluctant honesty.

chapters.title: The Choice of Keepers
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Both fleets offer him sanctuary in exchange for destroying or surrendering the archive. He refuses both, deciding instead to broadcast everything—garden logs, letters, manifests—to every ship in range. Emotional beat: quiet courage; choosing witness over weapon.

chapters.title: Broadcast
chapters.summary: Climax. As the truce expires, Gideon transmits the complete archive. Fleets power weapons; then crew decks begin receiving their own ancestors' names among the 'forged' passengers—refugees they thought lost. Uprisings of memory stall both commands. Emotional beat: breathless suspense breaking into collective grief.

chapters.title: What the Fleets Saw
chapters.summary: Oyelaran and Ashke POVs. Each privately confronts what the archive means: their fleets' founding myths were built on the same abandoned families. They meet again in the greenhouse, unarmed this time. Emotional beat: humbled reckoning; enemies recognizing shared inheritance.

chapters.title: The Charter of Meridian
chapters.summary: Ensemble. The fleets sign a new accord declaring Meridian neutral ground and living archive, its garden open to all descendants of the forged manifest. Gideon insists Mira be named co-keeper. Emotional beat: hard-won hope; bureaucracy transformed into belonging.

chapters.title: Log Entry 4,001
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. He records a new entry—not for absent colonists, but addressed to the arrivals docking below, the first people the garden was ever really for. Emotional beat: release; invisibility ended by choice, not force.

chapters.title: Greenhouse Full of Names
chapters.summary: Final chapter, ensemble. Planting season begins with volunteers from both fleets; each seedling is tagged with a name from the manifest. Gideon teaches, Mira keeps the records, and the station stops being a tomb. Emotional beat: warm resolution—found family rooted in tended soil.
